query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying single-pass friction stir processing (FSP) at sub-solidus temperatures to an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) with dual-phase lamellar colonies will refine its lamellae and disrupt crack-prone boundaries, thereby achieving higher room-temperature tensile ductility with retained or increased strength compared to the unmodified lamellar baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy with fine, dual-phase lamellar microstructure prone to microcracking under tensile loads.
generation.intervention: Single-pass friction stir processing using a rotating tool (e.g., 400–600 rpm) and a 25–50 mm/min traverse rate, ensuring the alloy remains in a solid-state regime below its eutectic melting temperature.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile tests are performed on friction-stir-processed samples after ensuring homogeneous stirring, consolidated material flow, and final thickness comparable to the baseline condition.
generation.structural_mediator: Refinement and partial breakup of lamellae by shear and dynamic recrystallization under FSP-induced shear deformation.
generation.mechanism: The friction stir tool shears and mechanically mixes the lamellar colonies, dispersing boundary defects and refining grains. Reduced intercolony interfaces impede microcrack initiation, while the refined microstructure enhances both strength (via dislocation and grain-boundary strengthening) and ductility (through more uniform plastic flow).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast lamellar baseline, the friction-stir-processed samples exhibit fewer early cracks at colony boundaries and show increased uniform elongation before fracture, with strength maintained or slightly improved.
generation.baseline: Unmodified as-cast lamellar colonies, where microcracks form along colony interfaces under room-temperature tensile loading, resulting in limited ductility despite high strength.
generation.boundary: Process temperature must remain below the eutectic melting point to avoid partial melting, and sufficient tool pressure is needed to prevent void formation. Excessive tool speed or multiple passes may overheat the alloy or cause localized damage.
generation.uncertainty: Direct evidence on friction stir processing of eutectic HEAs is not provided in the references, so additional data are needed to confirm the magnitude of ductility and strength improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical as-cast EHEA test bars. Subject half to friction stir processing under set tool rotation and travel speeds. Compare mechanical properties between processed and as-cast controls via standard room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility.
Microstructural characterization of lamellar spacing and grain size by SEM/TEM.
Fracture surface analysis (SEM) to identify microcrack initiation sites and fracture morphologies.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If friction-stir-processed samples do not exhibit finer, more homogeneous lamellae or show no improvement (or a decrease) in tensile strength and/or elongation relative to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

The bulk AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b . The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a . Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. decision.trend: Early work on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloys established that a fine lamellar microstructure can achieve impressive tensile strength and moderate ductility in as-cast or lightly cold-rolled conditions. However, despite modest improvements, internal lamellar boundaries remained sites for microcrack initiation and catastrophic fracture under room-temperature tension. No subsequent study in this lineage fully resolved the brittleness issue at ambient conditions.
decision.unsolved: How to mitigate microcracking in dual-phase lamellar stacks without sacrificing strength remains an open challenge. Although slight cold-rolling and heat treatment can raise strength, the gain typically comes at the expense of limited room-temperature tensile ductility. The persistent brittleness points to a need for processing routes that break up or reorganize the internal boundary network while preserving or enhancing the load-bearing capacity of the eutectic phases.
decision.lever: Single-pass friction stir processing of the as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy, using a rotating tool of appropriate geometry and speed to break up lamellae and refine boundary structures at sub-solidus temperatures
decision.why: The core hypothesis is that friction stir processing (FSP) at a controlled tool rotation speed (e.g., 400–600 rpm) and travel rate (e.g., 25–50 mm/min) will locally disrupt and refine the lamellar colony architecture, thereby reducing weak interfaces where microcracks originate and promoting more uniform plastic flow. Prior investigations in other multi-phase alloys show that FSP can produce ultra-fine grains and minimize crack-prone boundaries. Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, this FSP route is expected to increase tensile ductility while retaining or even raising strength via refined microstructure and enhanced strain hardening. Boundary conditions include maintaining the process temperature below the eutectic melt point for solid-state deformation and ensuring adequate tool shoulder pressure to consolidate the stirred region without introducing voids. A definitive experiment would be to compare the tension stress–strain behavior and fracture surfaces of friction-stir-processed versus as-cast specimens: persistence of early cracking in the FSP-treated region, with no enhancement in tensile elongation, would falsify the hypothesis.
